newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels say Mobutu agreed to discuss leaving.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels say Mobutu agreed to discuss leaving.

text.p: Zairean rebels, contradicting U.S. envoy Bill Richardson, said on Thursday President Mobutu Sese Seko agreed to discuss his departure from power in accepting face-to-face talks with rebel leader Laurent Kabila.
Rebel "Foreign Minister" Bizima Karaha told a news conference in Lubumbashi that Mobutu's departure was a prime condition for agreeing to the talks on a South African ship in international waters..
Adding to confusion over the timing of the talks, he told Reuters Kabila could only attend the talks on Sunday. "That is the time we have for the talks."
Shortly beforehand, South African President Nelson Mandela said through a spokesman that the talks, which he would chair, would take place on Friday.
Richardson said in Kinshasa on Wednesday, after seeing Mobutu, that there were no preconditions set for the encounter at sea.
Karaha said Kabila had decided the air should be cleared because Richardson "misled everyone".
Earlier on Thursday, Mobutu's camp said they understood the meeting was being postponed for a day until Saturday. The rebels said then they had not been informed of any change from Friday.
"We are happy that Mobutu has agreed to come and negotiate one and only one thing: his departure from power," Karaha said.

"This was a prime condition for the talks and we are happy to know negotiations will start and Mobutu has agreed to come and negotiate. He comes knowing full well what the terms of negotiations are: his departure," he added.
Karaha said Mobutu's departure would clear the way for other political arrangements in Zaire and allow the rebels to consider a ceasefire to end the civil war, which started last October.
"His departure will give way to other political arrangements and I must emphasise that we are not going to discuss a ceasefire before that," Karaha added.

"We thought it absolutely important to set the record straight. We have agreed to go to the talks and so has Mobutu on condition that only his departure will be subject to negotiations," Karaha added.
He said he was speaking with the authority of Kabila, who left Lubumbashi on Thursday for talks in neighbouring countries. A rebel official said he would return later the same day.
Kabila's original schedule was to visit neighbouring countries before flying to South Africa and then the talks.

Kabila, head of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, told Reuters late on Wednesday that when he met Mobutu they would discuss the president's departure from power after 32 years.
"The talks will just be about Mobutu and what we do with him. Our uncompromising demand is that he leaves power and we shall look after him," Kabila said.
He said Zairean troops had started blowing up bridges as rebels advanced on the town of Kenge on the way to Kinshasa.
A mining expert who arrived in Lubumbashi from the area on Thursday told Reuters rebels were advancing from the towns of Ilebo, Tshikapa, Kananga and Kikwit.

"It's big stuff. These guys are heavily equipped and should have no problems crossing the rivers in that area to Kenge and Kinshasa because they are equipped with bridge-laying gear and speedboats," he said.
The rebels have said they would enter Kinshasa within the next 10 to 15 days. The expert agreed: "From what I saw, that timescale makes a lot of sense. These guys are serious."
The rebel leader's aides said he had been surprised by Richardson's announcement in Kinshasa that "several African leaders" would attend the talks on the supply ship SAS Outeniqua.
The rebels do not want the talks to turn into a mini-summit about one of Africa's biggest political shake-ups for decades.
